vignette:
Patient: "Anna" (pseudonym)
Age: 31
Occupation: Paramedic
Trauma: Police violence (witnessed and directly threatened)

Anna comes into session already sitting on the edge of the chair, her work boots planted flat on the floor as if she might need to stand at any moment. She keeps her jacket on. She describes herself as someone who "used to be good at her job," which is the first thing she says, and then she stops.

The event happened fourteen months ago. Anna was on a night shift in a mid-sized city, dispatched to a welfare check that turned into a domestic disturbance. When she arrived, police were already on scene. She remembers stepping out of the ambulance, her partner behind her, and seeing an officer with his weapon drawn on a man who was already on the ground. The man was unarmed. Anna says she froze for a second, then started to move toward the patient-her training telling her to assess, to treat. A second officer turned and screamed at her. He told her to get back, to stay on the ground, to not move. She remembers the flashlight in her eyes, the way his voice cut through the sirens. She dropped to her knees. She put her hands in the air. She says she thought, They don't know I'm here to help. They see a threat.

She was held on the ground for what felt like ten minutes. Her partner was also detained. The man they had originally come to help was eventually taken away in handcuffs. No one was hurt by the police that night, Anna says, but she corrects herself: Except me.

In the months after, Anna started to feel something shift in her body. She began to dread the sound of a police radio crackling over her dispatch. She would flinch when she saw a cruiser in her rearview mirror. At first she told herself it was just the shock, that she would get over it. She had seen violence before-she had pulled people from car wrecks, held pressure on wounds, watched people die. But this was different. This was the people who were supposed to be on her side.

Now, at work, Anna is hypervigilant in a way she never was before. She scans scenes for uniforms before she exits the ambulance. She positions herself so she always has an exit route. She has stopped talking to police officers on scene unless absolutely necessary. Her partner has noticed. He asked her once if she was okay, and she said yes, because she didn't have words for what was happening.

At home, Anna is divorced. She says the marriage was already strained before the event, but afterward it became impossible. Her ex-husband didn't understand why she couldn't just "let it go." She would wake up at 3:00 a.m. with her heart pounding, convinced she heard shouting, convinced someone was in the house. She would check the locks three times. She stopped wanting him to touch her. She says she felt like she was living behind a sheet of glass.

She drinks now. Not every night, but most. She says it helps her fall asleep, even though she still wakes up. She has lost eight pounds in the last two months because she forgets to eat. She has stopped running, which used to be the thing that cleared her head.

The worst part, she says, is the shame. She is a paramedic. She is supposed to be the one who stays calm, who helps, who is in control. She feels like she failed that night, even though she knows intellectually she did nothing wrong. She replays the moment the officer screamed at her-the way her body obeyed before her mind could catch up. She hates that she dropped to her knees. She hates that she cried afterward in the ambulance.

She has not told anyone at work the full story. She told her supervisor it was "a stressful call," and he nodded and said to take a break. She took fifteen minutes. Then she went back out.

Anna's PCL-5 score is 44. She answered "Quite a bit" to the question about avoiding people or situations that remind her of the event. She answered "Extremely" to the question about feeling jumpy or easily startled. She answered "Moderately" to the question about having difficulty experiencing positive feelings.

She is here because she finally realized she cannot keep driving past police stations with her hands shaking. She is here because she wants to go back to being the person who knew what to do. She is not sure if that person still exists.
